drills.name: Blank-Sheet Fundamentals Dump
drills.whenToUse: Test unprompted retrieval for a fundamental you have previously studied.
steps: Dump everything from memory on [fundamental] covering: purpose, problem solved, terms, equations/relationships, operating values, field mistakes, and system recognition.
Audit the response into three categorized blocks: KNOWN, MISSING, and WRONG.
Rewrite only the MISSING and WRONG material from memory without looking at the corrections.
drills.whyItWorks: Uses no-lookup blank-page recall and error-based relearning. The second retrieval strengthens the exact material that failed.

drills.name: Rebuild the Loop From Memory
drills.whenToUse: Master signal paths and component interconnections automatically instead of memorizing isolated definitions.
steps: Reconstruct the entire signal path for [loop] from memory in sequence: Power source → Field device → Signal → Terminals/wiring → Input/output module → Controller → Final element.
Detail power origin, current/voltage path, signal type, component function, open-connection impact, and expected meter readings at two test points.
Compare your reconstructed path against the correct text diagram and review only the differences.
drills.whyItWorks: Uses chunking and dual coding by turning individual facts into a connected physical and signal-flow model.

drills.name: Spaced Fundamental Rotation
drills.whenToUse: Maintain long-term retention of previously studied fundamentals across days and weeks.
steps: Retrieve recall answers for a rotated set of 5 fundamentals one at a time.
Classify each response as SOLID (quick/correct), SLOW (hesitant), or MISS (incorrect/forgotten).
Re-test SLOW items later in the session, and re-test MISS items after two unrelated questions following a brief correction.
Schedule future reviews (1 day, 3 days, 1 week) focusing exclusively on weak items.
drills.whyItWorks: Uses spaced repetition and expanding retrieval while concentrating practice on weak memories instead of repeatedly reviewing known material.

drills.name: Build the Mental Model From Zero
drills.whenToUse: Convert superficial vocabulary familiarity into deep physical intuition.
steps: State what you believe [concept] means and describe the physical reality occurring in the field.
Anchor the model using a 1-sentence definition, simple text diagram, physical cause-and-effect relationship, key equation, and real field example.
Teach back the concept in your own words without referencing the original explanation.
drills.whyItWorks: Uses elaboration and teach-back. Reconstructing the physical mechanism creates a stronger anchor than memorizing definitions.

drills.name: Contrast Pair Drill
drills.whenToUse: Eliminate confusion when two related I&C concepts blend together.
steps: Define [concept A] and [concept B] from memory and state the key distinction in one sentence.
Categorize 6 short scenarios as A, B, BOTH, or NEITHER with a one-sentence justification for each.
Review a tailored comparison table containing only the distinctions you missed.
drills.whyItWorks: Uses interleaving and discriminative practice. The learner must identify which concept applies instead of recalling definitions in isolation.

drills.name: Instrument Principle to Real Device
drills.whenToUse: Connect theoretical physical principles to field devices and controller behavior.
steps: Map the missing measurement stages from memory: PROCESS CONDITION → Sensor → Transmitter → Signal → CONTROLLER VALUE.
Analyze a specific field instrument by answering: sensing quantity, internal conversion, output signal, controller interpretation, and installation error risks.
drills.whyItWorks: Uses dual coding and elaboration by connecting physical process behavior, sensing principle, signal conversion, and displayed value.

drills.name: 60-Second Fundamentals Sprint
drills.whenToUse: Speed up retrieval latency for known fundamental concepts.
steps: Answer 12 rapid-fire questions in ~5 seconds each (covering definitions, signals, equations, components, calculations, and what-if scenarios).
Track performance across CORRECT, HESITANT, and WRONG categories.
Retest HESITANT and WRONG items using newly worded questions.
drills.whyItWorks: Uses rapid-fire timed retrieval and error-based repetition to reduce recall latency under pressure.

drills.name: Blank Drawing Reconstruction
drills.whenToUse: Learn to mentally navigate control schematics and P&IDs without pre-labeled references.
steps: Draw a complete text schematic from memory based on a process description, including tags, symbols, signal types, direction, and controllers.
Audit the drawing for missing elements, incorrect signal flow, or symbol errors.
Redraw a second similar scenario without referencing earlier solutions.
drills.whyItWorks: Uses no-lookup reconstruction, dual coding, and error correction. Generating the drawing forces spatial and functional retrieval together.

drills.name: Operator Calls: What Do You Know?
drills.whenToUse: Practice loading correct core principles immediately when presented with a process complaint.
steps: List relevant measurement principles, signal ranges, devices involved, controller input, and necessary facts within 90 seconds of receiving a symptom.
Evaluate whether your recalled fundamentals support a logical diagnostic approach before attempting troubleshooting.
drills.whyItWorks: Uses retrieval under contextual pressure. It trains the habit of loading the correct mental model before acting on a symptom.

drills.name: Build and Prove a 4–20 mA Loop
drills.whenToUse: Mentally rehearse setting up, wiring, and calculating values across an analog loop.
steps: Specify device wiring type (2/3/4-wire), power source, supply voltage, current flow, receiver terminals, and meter test location.
Correct wiring errors inserted into a sample terminal diagram.
Calculate expected mA outputs across 0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100% process points, then convert given mA values back into span percentages.
drills.whyItWorks: Uses deliberate practice, calculation retrieval, and application to a physical loop instead of isolated 4–20 mA facts.

drills.name: Calibration Bench Simulation
drills.whenToUse: Practice transmitter calibration logic, error evaluation, and documentation.
steps: Calculate expected output values and tolerance limits for a 5-point calibration table (0% to 100%).
Judge as-found test data to classify zero errors, span errors, or linearity problems.
Document a final calibration log with as-found data, work performed, as-left results, and pass/fail status.
drills.whyItWorks: Uses deliberate practice and error classification. Calculating, judging tolerance, and documenting results links calibration theory to actual bench work.

drills.name: Touch the Loop: Measurement Point Drill
drills.whenToUse: Verify physical measurement expectations and meter placement at distinct circuit points.
steps: Predict expected readings across labeled test points (A, B, C, D) for voltage, current, resistance, or pressure.
Specify meter mode, lead placement, baseline reading, and diagnosis for abnormal high/low values.
Identify an intentionally unsafe or invalid measurement practice inserted into the drill.
drills.whyItWorks: Uses applied retrieval and elaboration. The learner must connect circuit theory to an actual measurement location and expected observation.

drills.name: Evidence Before Cause
drills.whenToUse: Eliminate guessing by using diagnostic measurements to isolate system faults systematically.
steps: Select one diagnostic check based solely on an initial symptom.
Analyze test results by declaring: OBSERVATION (what showed), PROVES (conclusions), DOES NOT PROVE (remaining causes), and NEXT CHECK.
Isolate the exact fault without replacing evidence with assumptions.
drills.whyItWorks: Uses error-based learning and deliberate diagnostic practice. Each measurement must reduce uncertainty rather than simply generate activity.

drills.name: Fault Path From a Blank Page
drills.whenToUse: Construct a logical troubleshooting tree before evaluating physical diagnostic choices.
steps: Map a blank-page fault tree: SYMPTOM → Expected Behavior → Proving Signal → Test Location → Next Step (Present/Absent).
Critique the efficiency and signal-path logic of your chosen testing order.
drills.whyItWorks: Uses no-lookup recall and chunking. Building the diagnostic tree strengthens a reusable signal-path troubleshooting model.

drills.name: Inject One Fault
drills.whenToUse: Recognize specific fault symptoms by analyzing behavior in a baseline-healthy system.
steps: Establish baseline conditions for process, field device, signal, PLC, and final element.
Diagnose a hidden injected fault based strictly on resulting symptom output.
Verify the affected system layer, supporting observations, and confirming tests.
drills.whyItWorks: Uses error-based learning and causal reasoning. Symptoms become attached to system behavior instead of memorized as disconnected fault lists.

drills.name: One-Page Fundamental From Memory
drills.whenToUse: Build a concise field reference sheet while testing recall completeness.
steps: Draft a one-page reference from memory using: PURPOSE, CORE PRINCIPLE, NORMAL VALUES, BASIC DIAGRAM, FIELD CHECKS, COMMON FAILURES, and ONE RULE.
Audit the draft by marking each item as KEEP, CORRECT, or ADD.
Finalize a compressed 2-minute field reference containing a practical example.
drills.whyItWorks: Uses blank-page recall, compression, and generation. Creating the reference before seeing the answer exposes weak knowledge instead of hiding it.

drills.name: Signal Chain Compression
drills.whenToUse: Simplify complex systems down to essential functional stages and energy boundaries.
steps: Compress the system into max 7 functional blocks (Process → Sensor → Transmitter → Signal → Controller → Output → Final Element).
Annotate each connecting arrow with the physical quantity crossing the boundary (pressure, mA, VDC, air psi, etc.).
Target which block to investigate first for a given symptom.
drills.whyItWorks: Uses chunking and dual coding. Compression separates functional stages while preserving the physical signal relationships between them.

drills.name: Build the Pocket Tables
drills.whenToUse: Commit high-frequency baseline numbers and scaling ratios to automatic memory.
steps: Fill in quick-reference values from memory for 4–20 mA points (0–100%), Ohm's law formulas, span/LRV/URV equations, and sensor principles.
Verify responses against the corrected pocket reference table.
Apply at least two values from memory to solve a practical field scenario.

traps.trap: Starting with the meter instead of the drawing
traps.looksLike: You grab a multimeter and start poking. You have no hypothesis.
traps.fix: Always start with the loop drawing or P&ID. Trace the signal on paper first. Then verify in the field.

traps.looksLike: The reading looks off, so you replace the transmitter. The real problem was a blocked impulse line or a loose wire.
traps.fix: Verify the entire loop before condemning a device. Check impulse lines, wiring, and power before swapping hardware.

traps.looksLike: The PLC reads 0 mA and you assume the transmitter failed. The loop power supply tripped.
traps.fix: Check loop power first. A 0 mA reading on a 2-wire loop usually means the loop is broken, not that the transmitter is dead.

traps.looksLike: You calibrate a transmitter without checking as-found data. You have no idea if it was actually out of spec.
traps.fix: Record as-found before you adjust anything. The calibration record is your evidence, not just paperwork.

traps.looksLike: A motor will not start. You check the motor and starter. The problem was a closed permissive in the PLC logic.
traps.fix: When a final element will not actuate, check the PLC logic permissives before you touch the field device.

traps.looksLike: You wire a sensor to a PLC input card and get no signal. The card is sourcing, the sensor is sinking (or vice versa).
traps.fix: Know your card type before you wire. This is one of the most common 24 VDC mistakes.

traps.trap: Tuning a loop before understanding the process
traps.looksLike: You adjust PID parameters without knowing how far the process variable is allowed to move.
traps.fix: Ask operations: "How far and how fast am I allowed to let this variable move?" before you tune anything.

traps.looksLike: You cannot find an instrument because you are looking for the wrong tag.
traps.fix: Learn ISA 5.1 tag format. The first letter tells you the measured variable. The second tells you the function.

wireItLive.title: 24 VDC Three-Wire Start/Stop Control
operation: Press START: CR coil energizes, aux contact 13-14 closes in parallel with START, coil stays energized after release.
Press STOP: NC contact opens, breaks the coil holding path, CR drops out, CR contact 23-24 opens, M coil drops out, motor stops.
OL tripping opens the same coil path as STOP.
The diode suppresses the inductive voltage spike when CR coil de-energizes (protects PLC inputs and adjacent contacts).

faults.name: Missing seal-in contact
faults.consequence: coil energizes only while START is held; drops immediately on release.

faults.name: STOP wired as NO
faults.consequence: pressing STOP energizes instead of breaking; circuit cannot be stopped from the pushbutton.

faults.name: Diode reversed
faults.consequence: anode to A1, cathode to A2. Applying 24V short-circuits through the forward-biased diode; PSU folds back.

faults.name: OL in the wrong position (after CR coil)
faults.consequence: motor overload no longer drops the control relay; the safety function fails.

faults.name: Broken wire in the seal-in parallel branch
faults.consequence: CR latches but drops the moment START releases.

readingTheResult: 1. mA dev bad, HMI dev matches it: problem is upstream of the card (injection, wiring, card input).
2. mA dev good, HMI dev bad: signal arrives correctly; suspect scaling (LRV/URV/units) in the controller.
